item.title: Webb Captures Stars in the Early Stages of Life in a Nearby Stellar Nursery
item.description: This Webb infrared image, released on October 6th, 2026, shows the star-forming region NGC 7129, about 3,300 light-years from Earth. The central star, LkHα 234, is a young star of 5–8 solar masses whose outflows have cleared a cavity about 3.5 light-years across. On the right side of the region, younger protostars shoot jets of very hot material that create shocks in the surrounding gas.

item.title: Supernova Explosions First Aided, Then Later Impeded, the Epoch of Reionization
item.description: The Epoch of Reionization is when radiation from early galaxies and their stars reionized neutral hydrogen and let light travel freely through the cosmos. Some research shows that supernovae helped the process. But new research shows that, though they may have helped initially, supernovae eventually slowed reionization.

item.title: Hubble observations challenge supernova winds' role in cosmic reionization
item.description: An international team of researchers, including members from the University of Michigan, has revealed surprising results that could rewrite our understanding of a key transition in the early universe.

item.title: Black hole observations uncover evidence of solar storm–like magnetic eruptions
item.description: Technion researchers have presented evidence for the existence of solar-storm-like outbursts near supermassive black holes, which can be a million times larger than the sun or more. The phenomenon was discovered in the vicinity of the black hole in the galaxy NGC 3783, and the researchers' findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

item.title: Are 'mega-Earths' real? Stellar activity may explain these oversized rocky worlds
item.description: A new study suggests that some of the heaviest rocky planets ever reported may not be as heavy as they look. These so-called 'mega-Earths,' rocky planets weighing more than about 10 Earths, could be an illusion created by activity on their host stars. The paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Oct. 8.

item.title: Astronomers uncover the engine behind the most powerful stellar flares in the Kepler field
item.description: A new study led by researchers at the Konkoly Observatory of the HUN-REN Research Centre for Astronomy and Earth Sciences (HUN-REN CSFK) in Budapest has revealed what makes a distant red giant star the most explosively active in the entire Kepler field—and the answer lies in a surprisingly subtle interplay between a close stellar companion, vast dark starspots and a highly efficient internal magnetic dynamo.

item.title: A magnetar can be born when two neutron stars touch
item.description: All neutron stars have intense magnetic fields. The typical magnetic field of a neutron star is about 100,000 times stronger than the strongest magnetic fields we can create on Earth. But about 1% of neutron stars have even stronger magnetic fields. Known as magnetars, their magnetic fields can be 1,000 times stronger than a regular magnetic field. item.title: A pulsar's apparent slowdown reveals a rare stellar trio
item.description: Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars, the extremely dense cores left behind when massive stars explode. Astrophysicists have recently observed a pulsar rotating over 300 times per second that appeared to be slowing down unusually quickly.

item.title: JWST tours Orion’s hidden stellar nursery
item.description: Few sights thrill backyard observers as much as the Orion Nebula (M42). The brightest stellar nursery visible from mid-northern latitudes resolves into a complex web of luminous gas and dusty tendrils even through modest telescopes. item.title: The sun may have stripped away meters of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS
item.description: The interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS brought material from another planetary system within reach of our telescopes, but reading its chemistry poses a problem. Energetic particles encountered during its journey through space may have changed its outer layers, so how much of what astronomers detect still reflects the comet's birthplace?

item.title: The Chemistry in Stellar Nurseries is Complex, and a New 3D Model Highlights It
item.description: Young stars form in molecular clouds, and once they're turned on, they begin to shape their natal clouds with radiation. Researchers developed a new 3D model of one feature of the Orion Nebula star-forming region called the Orion Bar. Their model matches JWST observations, and explains how the uneven structure in stellar nurseries creates shadowed regions that alters the astrochemistry in the clouds.

item.title: Pair of distinct black hole mergers sheds new light on nature of their formation and evolution
item.description: The mergers, measured one month apart in 2024 by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration, advance scientific understanding of the nature of black hole formation and fundamental physics. A pair of distant cosmic black hole mergers, measured just one month apart in late 2024, is improving how scientists understand the nature and evolution of the most violent deep-space collisions […]

item.title: Impossibly fast-moving stars are revealing the Milky Way’s mysterious heart
item.description: Near the centre of the Milky Way, a swarm of stars hurtles around a supermassive black hole at extraordinary speeds. Studying them could be the key to understanding our galaxy

item.title: Using wobbling stellar material, astronomers measure the spin of a supermassive black hole for the first time
item.description: The results offer a new way to probe supermassive black holes and their evolution across the universe.
